Thank you for submitting your article "Specialization of the Chromatin Remodeler RSC to Mobilize Partially-Unwrapped Nucleosomes" for consideration by eLife. Your article has been reviewed by three peer reviewers, one of whom is a member of our Board of Reviewing Editors, and the evaluation has been overseen by Kevin Struhl as the Senior Editor. The following individual involved in review of your submission has agreed to reveal their identity: Blaine Bartholomew (Reviewer #3).

The reviewers appreciated the new experiments and additional statistical analysis done in response to their comments. I'm happy to say they all agree that the revised paper will be appropriate for eLife with just a few additional changes to the text. This letter is to help you prepare a revised submission.

The reviewers state that this paper has several key results that are solid and significant:

1) The RSC1 enzyme has evolved to use the Rsc3/30 module, and this module facilitates expression of RP genes and helps to counteract histone substitution alleles. Surprisingly, this module has an inhibitory impact in vitro on both enzymes.

2) Hmo1 functions together with RSC1 and RSC2 (though more so with RSC2) to facilitate nucleosome sliding in vitro and gene expression.

3) Rsc1 and Rsc2 show distinct genetic interactions with histone residues.

4) The functional interactions between Rsc1, Rsc2, Hmo1, and Rsc3/30 are enlightening.

5) RSC1 remodels a 5S nucleosome much better than RSC2, though they show more equivalent activity on a 601 nucleosome.

However, the one concern that remains is whether the paper over-simplifies things by making the strong, generalized conclusion (stated in the title and at various points in the paper) that the differential activity of RSC1 and RSC2 is linked to partial unwrapping of the nucleosome. Although the genetic evidence is consistent with your model, reviewer 2 (supported by reviewer 3) cites published data saying the difference in 5S versus 601 unwrapping is not as clear as suggested in your text:

"Introduction. The authors cite 4 papers in support of the statement that "entry/exit DNA displays higher level of detachment from the octamer" (for 5S in comparison to 601). However, none of these papers compare 5S to 601. Polach and Widom, 1995 used 5S, and Li and Widom, 2004 used 601. In the cited review (Zhou et al., 2019), they discuss in detail the comprehensive study by the Poirier group (North et al., 2012; not cited) where they do directly compare 5S and 601 nucleosomes in FRET-based unwrapping assays. Contrary to expectations, a 5S nucleosome unwraps less than 601 at the edge. This is shown to be due to the first 7bp of the 5S sequence at the entry/exit site. Thus, even though 601 has a higher overall affinity, the unwrapping dynamics are higher than 5S. These data are also consistent with published work showing that the 5S sequence has a higher affinity for H2A/H2B dimers (cited in Zhou et al., 2019). Notably, the higher affinity of 601 for octamers is due to AT repeats surrounding the dyad (and contacting the H3/H4 tetramer), not really the edges. As discussed by the authors, differences in how they interpret their data and other work (e.g., older Owen-Hughes work on α N-helix substitutions) may be due to the differences in histone octamer source – yeast vs Xenopus. Perhaps yeast dimers have a higher affinity for 601, rather than 5S. However, without extensive discussion, the authors' current conclusions seem to contradict several previously published papers. In general, the remodeling assays don't support a simple model where RSC1 remodels unwrapped nucleosomes better than RSC2. Note that I am not questioning the data at all – they are solid and very well done. I worry that the conclusions may just not be so simple."

In your revised manuscript, please address this point. I took a look at the paper cited by the reviewer (North et al., 10215) and it does seem to claim that 601 unwraps its ends more that 5S. If the reviewer's summary of the literature is accurate, please modify your statements (and model Figure 6) concerning 5S versus 601 accordingly, and factor that into your discussion and interpretations. If you feel those results can be reconciled, or are not applicable, to your model, please explain why in your Discussion section.

claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from stringency testing shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: The CT2 domain of Rsc1 mediates preferential association with Rsc3/30.
claims.source: To identify whether a particular region within Rsc1 mediates this preferential association with Rsc3/30, we performed domain swaps between Rsc1 and Rsc2 (Figure 1C) and checked for complementation and Rsc3 association.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from domain swap experiments and co-immunoprecipitation assays (Figure 1C-E).

claims.claim: Co-immunoprecipitation revealed strong Rsc3 association with Rsc1, and with Rsc2 derivatives only if they contained the CT2 region of Rsc1.
claims.source: Here, co-immunoprecipitation revealed strong Rsc3 association with Rsc1, and with Rsc2 derivatives only if they contained the CT2 region of Rsc1 (Figure 1E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from co-immunoprecipitation assays shown in Figure 1E.

claims.claim: Strong Rsc3 association with Rsc1 was lost when Rsc1 contained the CT2 region of Rsc2.
claims.source: Conversely, strong Rsc3 association with Rsc1 was lost when Rsc1 contained the CT2 region of Rsc2.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from co-immunoprecipitation assays shown in Figure 1E.

claims.claim: The region on Rsc1 responsible for strong Rsc3/30 association is narrowed to residues 617–777.
claims.source: Similar approaches involving internal Rsc1/2 deletions and additional swap positions provided further refinement, narrowing the region on Rsc1 responsible for strong Rsc3/30 association to residues 617–777 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from deletion and domain swap experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: Several structures of RSC-nucleosome complexes have recently been published.
claims.source: Several structures of RSC-nucleosome complexes have recently been published (Wagner et al., 2020; Ye et al., 2019; Patel et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to recent structural studies.

claims.claim: Rsc1, Rsc2, Rsc3, and Rsc30 are within the flexible regions of RSC-nucleosome structures, and these structures contain only partial models (or lack density/models).
claims.source: However, as Rsc1, Rsc2, Rsc3, and Rsc30 are within the flexible regions, these structures contain only partial models (or lack density/models).
claims.evidence: This statement is based on analysis of published structures and represents an inference about the structural flexibility of these subunits.

claims.claim: While the Rsc1-Rsc3/30 interaction has not been resolved structurally, crosslinks were observed between Rsc2 CT2 and Rsc3/30 heterodimer.
claims.source: While the Rsc1-Rsc3/30 interaction has not been resolved structurally, crosslinks were observed between Rsc2 CT2 and Rsc3/30 heterodimer (Wagner et al., 2020), an interaction we find to be much stronger in Rsc1.
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work and by the experimental data presented in this manuscript.

claims.claim: All four RSC complexes (RSC1+3/30, RSC1-3/30, RSC2+3/30, RSC2-3/30) displayed similar DNA-dependent ATPase activities in typical Vmax determinations with plasmid DNA.
claims.source: First, all four RSC complexes displayed similar DNA-dependent ATPase activities in typical Vmax determinations with plasmid DNA (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from ATPase assays shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: The activity of RSC1-3/30 complex plateaued earlier than the other RSC complexes in ATPase assays.
claims.source: The activity of one complex, RSC1-3/30, plateaued earlier than the other RSC complexes, but otherwise the two complexes behaved similarly.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from ATPase assays shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: RSC1 complex displayed much greater sliding activity than RSC2 on 5S nucleosomes.
claims.source: However, major differences were observed with 5S nucleosomes – RSC1 complex displayed much greater sliding activity than RSC2 (Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1 for quantification).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from nucleosome sliding assays shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: All sliding activities with RSC1 and RSC2 complexes are ATP dependent.
claims.source: As shown previously for RSC, all sliding activities with RSC1 and RSC2 complexes are ATP dependent (Cairns et al., 1996 and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work and by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claims.claim: RSC1 and RSC2 complexes both bound 5S nucleosomes comparably in the absence of ATP.
claims.source: RSC1 and RSC2 complexes both bound 5S nucleosomes comparably in the absence of ATP (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B) indicating that their differences in activities occur after the initial engagement of the 5S nucleosome.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from nucleosome binding assays shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B.

claims.claim: The differences in remodeling activities between RSC1 and RSC2 complexes occur after the initial engagement of the 5S nucleosome.
claims.source: RSC1 and RSC2 complexes both bound 5S nucleosomes comparably in the absence of ATP (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B) indicating that their differences in activities occur after the initial engagement of the 5S nucleosome.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that RSC1 and RSC2 bind nucleosomes similarly but remodel them differently.

claims.claim: The Rsc3/30 module did not affect ATPase activities of RSC1 or RSC2 complexes.
claims.source: Finally, the Rsc3/30 module did not affect their ATPase activities (Figure 2B) nor their binding to 5S nucleosomes (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B); however, in both the RSC1 and RSC2 complexes, Rsc3/30 inclusion moderately inhibited remodeling (Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from ATPase assays shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: The Rsc3/30 module did not affect binding of RSC1 or RSC2 complexes to 5S nucleosomes.
claims.source: Finally, the Rsc3/30 module did not affect their ATPase activities (Figure 2B) nor their binding to 5S nucleosomes (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B); however, in both the RSC1 and RSC2 complexes, Rsc3/30 inclusion moderately inhibited remodeling (Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from nucleosome binding assays shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B.

claims.claim: In both the RSC1 and RSC2 complexes, Rsc3/30 inclusion moderately inhibited remodeling of 5S nucleosomes.
claims.source: Finally, the Rsc3/30 module did not affect their ATPase activities (Figure 2B) nor their binding to 5S nucleosomes (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B); however, in both the RSC1 and RSC2 complexes, Rsc3/30 inclusion moderately inhibited remodeling (Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from nucleosome sliding assays shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: The slower-migrating RSC remodeled product on native gels is an intact nucleosome, not a hexasome or tetrasome.
claims.source: Here, the 'slid' band maintained a dimer to DNA ratio similar to the starting nucleosome, rather than that predicted for a hexasome or tetrasome, supporting the identity of the slower-migrating band being an intact nucleosome.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from sliding assays with fluorescently labeled H2A shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claims.claim: Histone mutations that are lethal specifically with rsc1Δ mapped exclusively within the H3 αN helix region – the position where DNA enters/exits the nucleosome.
claims.source: In striking contrast, those mutations that were lethal specifically with rsc1Δ mapped exclusively within the H3 αN helix region – the position where DNA enters/exits the nucleosome (Table 1, Figure 3A–B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from genetic screens shown in Table 1 and Figure 3A-B.

claims.claim: The specific H3 αN helix mutations obtained in the screen overlap strongly with those reported to increase partial unwrapping using FRET formats.
claims.source: Furthermore, the specific H3 αN helix mutations obtained in our screen overlap strongly with those reported to increase partial unwrapping using FRET formats (Ferreira et al., 2007), whereas alanine substitutions that did not show a phenotype (P43A, E50A, K56A) had little effect on FRET/unwrapping (Table 2).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of the genetic screen data with published FRET data, shown in Table 2.

claims.claim: Alanine substitutions that did not show a phenotype in the genetic screen (P43A, E50A, K56A) had little effect on FRET/unwrapping.
claims.source: Furthermore, the specific H3 αN helix mutations obtained in our screen overlap strongly with those reported to increase partial unwrapping using FRET formats (Ferreira et al., 2007), whereas alanine substitutions that did not show a phenotype (P43A, E50A, K56A) had little effect on FRET/unwrapping (Table 2).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of the genetic screen data with published FRET data, shown in Table 2.

claims.claim: rsc1Δ shows synthetic lethality primarily with mutations in the H2A C-terminus which interact with the H3 αN helix, as well as with specific histone-DNA contacts (H2A R78 and H2A R30).
claims.source: In keeping with the results above, we find rsc1Δ-specific synthetic lethality primarily with mutations in the H2A C-terminus which interact with the H3 αN helix, as well as with specific histone-DNA contacts (H2A R78 and H2A R30; Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from genetic screens with H2A-H2B mutations shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Synthetic lethality in rsc1∆ strains is due to decreased ability of RSC2 complexes to remodel partially-unwrapped nucleosomes relative to RSC1 complexes.
claims.source: Taken together, our genetic results, which encompass the entire nucleosome, strongly suggest that synthetic lethality in rsc1∆ strains is due to decreased ability of RSC2 complexes to remodel partially-unwrapped nucleosomes relative to RSC1 complexes.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the genetic screen data showing that rsc1Δ-specific synthetic lethal mutations map to regions involved in DNA entry/exit from the nucleosome.

claims.claim: The CT2 domain of Rsc1, which interacts better with Rsc3/30 than its counterpart in Rsc2, confers growth when placed within a Rsc2 derivative in combination with histone αN helix mutations.
claims.source: Here, growth was clearly restored to rsc1Δ H3 G44A and rsc1Δ H3 R40A combinations with a plasmid encoding Rsc1 or Rsc2 bearing the Rsc1 CT2, but not with Rsc2 or Rsc1 bearing the Rsc2 CT2 (Figure 3C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from complementation assays shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: Additional domain swap experiments localize the complementation of rsc1Δ αN helix histone combined lethality to the Rsc3/30 association region in Rsc1 (aa 617–777).
claims.source: Additional domain swap experiments localize this complementation to the Rsc3/30 association region in Rsc1 (aa 617–777) (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from domain swap experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A.

claims.claim: High-copy RSC3 or RSC30 suppresses the strong temperature sensitivity (Ts-) phenotype of rsc1Δ H3 V46A.
claims.source: While high-copy RSC3 or RSC30 could not rescue rsc1Δ αN helix histone combined lethality (data not shown), suppression of the strong temperature sensitivity (Ts-) phenotype of rsc1Δ H3 V46A was observed (Figure 3D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from high-copy suppression assays shown in Figure 3D.

claims.claim: Improving the association/functionality of Rsc3/30 suppresses phenotypes associated with αN helix histone mutations.
claims.source: Taken together, improving the association/functionality of Rsc3/30 suppresses phenotypes associated with αN helix histone mutations – further linking Rsc1/2 and Rsc3/30 to partial nucleosome unwrapping.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the complementation and suppression experiments.

claims.claim: The H3 K56A mutation was not lethal in combination with either rsc1Δ or rsc2Δ.
claims.source: However, the H3 K56A mutation was not lethal in combination with either rsc1Δ or rsc2Δ (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from genetic screens shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: The H3 K56Q mutation confers synthetic lethality when combined with rsc1Δ, but not with rsc2Δ.
claims.source: The K56Q mutation confers synthetic lethality when combined with rsc1Δ, but not with rsc2Δ (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from genetic assays shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B.

claims.claim: Domain swaps involving the highly homologous bromodomains and BAH domains between Rsc1 and Rsc2 did not confer phenotypic differences, nor did these swaps alter the synthetic lethality of rsc1Δ with histone αN helix mutations.
claims.source: Furthermore, domain swaps involving the highly homologous bromodomains and BAH domains between Rsc1 and Rsc2 did not confer phenotypic differences, nor did these swaps alter the synthetic lethality of rsc1Δ with histone αN helix mutations (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from domain swap experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A.

claims.claim: H3 K56A has little effect on DNA unwrapping, whereas K56Q promotes unwrapping.
claims.source: Notably, H3 K56A has little effect on DNA unwrapping, whereas K56Q promotes unwrapping (Ferreira et al., 2007; Masumoto et al., 2005) – and is lethal with rsc1Δ, further supporting an unwrapping function as being responsible for the phenotype.
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work and by the genetic data presented in this manuscript.

claims.claim: The lethality of H3 K56Q with rsc1Δ does not appear linked to bromodomains or histone acetylation.
claims.source: Thus, the lethality with rsc1Δ does not appear linked to bromodomains or histone acetylation, in agreement with findings that H3K56 acetylation does not enhance RSC binding (Neumann et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the domain swap experiments and is supported by a citation to prior work.

claims.claim: Although sliding of nucleosomes bearing H3 R40A by either form of RSC is reduced relative to wild-type (WT) 5S nucleosomes, RSC1 complexes were markedly more active than RSC2 complexes.
claims.source: Although sliding of nucleosomes bearing H3 R40A by either form of RSC is reduced relative to wild-type (WT) 5S nucleosomes, RSC1 complexes were markedly more active than RSC2 complexes (Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 3 for quantification), reinforcing the difference between RSC1 and RSC2.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from nucleosome sliding assays shown in Figure 3E.

claims.claim: Both RSC1 and RSC2 complexes bind H3 αN helix mutant 5S nucleosomes similarly.
claims.source: Additionally, both RSC1 and RSC2 complexes bind H3 αN helix mutant 5S nucleosomes similarly (Figure 3—figure supplement 4), demonstrating that initial nucleosome binding is not inhibited by this octamer mutation, suggesting downstream remodeling activity as the affected step.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from nucleosome binding assays shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claims.claim: Initial nucleosome binding is not inhibited by the H3 R40A octamer mutation, suggesting downstream remodeling activity as the affected step.
claims.source: Additionally, both RSC1 and RSC2 complexes bind H3 αN helix mutant 5S nucleosomes similarly (Figure 3—figure supplement 4), demonstrating that initial nucleosome binding is not inhibited by this octamer mutation, suggesting downstream remodeling activity as the affected step.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that RSC1 and RSC2 bind H3 R40A nucleosomes similarly but remodel them differently.

claims.claim: WT 174 bp 5S yeast nucleosomes display a fully-wrapped side (position 158), and a side of partial unwrapping, in agreement with asymmetric 5S nucleosome unwrapping previously shown.
claims.source: We found WT 174 bp 5S yeast nucleosomes display a fully-wrapped side (position 158), and a side of partial unwrapping, in agreement with asymmetric 5S nucleosome unwrapping previously shown (Winogradoff and Aksimentiev, 2019; Chen et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from ExoIII-S1 nuclease mapping shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 5 and by citations to prior work.

claims.claim: WT nucleosomes displayed a much higher proportion of largely-wrapped species (≥135 bp) than did H3 R40A nucleosomes.
claims.source: Here, WT nucleosomes displayed a much higher proportion of largely-wrapped species (≥135 bp) than did H3 R40A nucleosomes (Figure 3—figure supplement 5).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from ExoIII-S1 nuclease mapping shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 5.

claims.claim: The mapping data support the hypothesis that RSC1 complexes manage partially-unwrapped nucleosomes better than RSC2 complexes.
claims.source: Since RSC2 is more deficient than RSC1 in repositioning H3 R40A nucleosomes, the mapping supports the hypothesis that RSC1 complexes manage partially-unwrapped nucleosomes better than RSC2 complexes.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the nuclease mapping and remodeling data.

claims.claim: H3 R40A 5S nucleosomes are likely to have a distinct conformation that is not distinguished in the nuclease protection assay.
claims.source: We note that H3 R40A 5S nucleosomes are likely to have a distinct conformation that is not distinguished in our nuclease protection assay, since remodeling by both RSC1 and (more so) by RSC2 complexes is inhibited by the H3 αN helix mutation (compare Figure 3E with Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that H3 R40A nucleosomes are remodeled less efficiently than WT nucleosomes.

claims.claim: H3 R40A mutant octamers may enforce a greater degree of openness or distance between the 5S DNA ends, and thereby inhibit RSC activity.
claims.source: These mutant octamers may enforce a greater degree of openness or distance between the 5S DNA ends, as demonstrated previously (Ferreira et al., 2007), and thereby inhibit RSC activity (perhaps the transition of binding to DNA translocation, see Discussion) – a nucleosome perturbation better managed by RSC1 complexes.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative statement about the mechanism by which H3 R40A affects RSC activity, supported by a citation to prior work.

claims.claim: Hmo1 is an HMGB family protein that stabilizes fragile/partially-unwrapped nucleosomes, particularly at rRNA and ribosomal protein gene promoters.
claims.source: Hmo1 is an HMGB family protein that stabilizes fragile/partially-unwrapped nucleosomes, particularly at rRNA and ribosomal protein gene promoters (Hall et al., 2006; Panday and Grove, 2017).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work characterizing Hmo1 function.

claims.claim: Unlike other HMGB proteins which have an acidic CTD that promotes bending and nucleosome destabilization, Hmo1 is unique in containing a basic lysine rich C-terminal extension, and has been shown to stabilize chromatin and perform the functions of a linker histone.
claims.source: Unlike other HMGB proteins which have an acidic CTD that promotes bending and nucleosome destabilization, Hmo1 is unique in containing a basic lysine rich C-terminal extension, and has been shown to stabilize chromatin and perform the functions of a linker histone (Panday and Grove, 2016).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work characterizing Hmo1 structure and function.

claims.claim: Hmo1 is proposed to bind near the nucleosome dyad and use its basic extension to bind linker DNA and prevent bending.
claims.source: Hmo1 is proposed to bind near the nucleosome dyad and use its basic extension to bind linker DNA and prevent bending (Panday and Grove, 2017), which may also improve wrapping and thus cooperate with RSC1 or RSC2 to promote remodeling.
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work and includes speculation about how Hmo1 might cooperate with RSC.

claims.claim: Synthetic phenotypes are observed in rsc1Δ hmo1Δ mutants, but not rsc2Δ hmo1Δ mutants.
claims.source: Notably, we observe synthetic phenotypes in rsc1Δ hmo1Δ mutants, but not rsc2Δ hmo1Δ mutants (Figure 4A), suggesting a greater reliance of Rsc2 on Hmo1 for functional cooperativity.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from genetic interaction assays shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: The rsc1Δ hmo1Δ synthetic sickness suggests a greater reliance of Rsc2 on Hmo1 for functional cooperativity.
claims.source: Notably, we observe synthetic phenotypes in rsc1Δ hmo1Δ mutants, but not rsc2Δ hmo1Δ mutants (Figure 4A), suggesting a greater reliance of Rsc2 on Hmo1 for functional cooperativity.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the genetic interaction data.

claims.claim: The rsc1Δ hmo1Δ synthetic sickness is partially complemented by the presence of the Rsc1 CT2, and partially suppressed by high-copy RSC3 or RSC30.
claims.source: Furthermore, as we saw with the H3 αN helix mutations, this synthetic sickness was partially complemented by the presence of the Rsc1 CT2, and partially suppressed by high-copy RSC3 or RSC30, providing further support that these proteins work together in a modular manner (Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from complementation and suppression assays shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: Both Rsc1 and Rsc2 co-immunoprecipitate with Hmo1, which represents either a direct interaction between Hmo1 and RSC or colocalization on the same nucleosome(s).
claims.source: Immunoprecipitation with anti-Myc or anti-V5 antibody followed by immunoblot analysis revealed that both Rsc1 and Rsc2 co-immunoprecipitate with Hmo1, which represents either a direct interaction between Hmo1 and RSC or colocalization on the same nucleosome(s) (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from co-immunoprecipitation assays shown in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: Hmo1 shows physical interaction on chromatin with Rsc1 and Rsc2, but strong functional/genetic interaction primarily with Rsc2.
claims.source: Taken together, Hmo1 shows physical interaction on chromatin with Rsc1 and Rsc2, but strong functional/genetic interaction primarily with Rsc2 (RSC2 complexes are reliant on Hmo1, in a rsc1Δ strain).
claims.evidence: This is a summary statement integrating the co-IP and genetic interaction data.

claims.claim: Hmo1 stimulates the sliding activity of RSC and SWI/SNF complex in vitro on 601 nucleosomes.
claims.source: Hmo1 stimulates the sliding activity of RSC and SWI/SNF complex in vitro on 601 nucleosomes (Hepp et al., 2014), but it is not known whether stimulation applies equally to RSC1 and RSC2 complexes, or has a differential effect on their action upon partially-unwrapped nucleosomes.
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claims.claim: Hmo1 moderately stimulates RSC1 activity, whereas Hmo1 greatly stimulates RSC2 activity on 5S nucleosomes.
claims.source: Interestingly, Hmo1 moderately stimulates RSC1 activity, whereas Hmo1 greatly stimulates RSC2 activity (Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 2 for quantification), a property that is even more evident in conditions of limiting remodeler or at early time points (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from nucleosome sliding assays with Hmo1 shown in Figure 4D.

claims.claim: Both RSC1 and RSC2 slide the 5S nucleosome at lower remodeler concentrations in the presence of Hmo1.
claims.source: Moreover, both RSC1 and RSC2 slide the 5S nucleosome at lower remodeler concentrations in the presence of Hmo1 (30 nM RSC without Hmo1 compare with 10 nM RSC with Hmo1), further supporting a role for Hmo1 in stimulating RSC remodeling activity.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from nucleosome sliding assays with Hmo1 shown in Figure 4D.

claims.claim: RSC1 and RSC2 complexes both displayed robust sliding activity with 601 nucleosomes, with RSC1 activity slightly higher.
claims.source: Here, RSC1 and RSC2 complexes both displayed robust sliding activity with 601 nucleosomes, with RSC1 activity slightly higher (Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 4 for quantification).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from nucleosome sliding assays shown in Figure 4E.

claims.claim: There is a correlation between ejection and the use of strong positioning sequences – their initial stability from favored 'phasing' may convert to high instability and disfavored 'phasing' after 5 bp of DNA translocation – which may underlie the progressive ejection observed with 601 nucleosomes.
claims.source: We note a correlation here and in prior work (Clapier et al., 2016) between ejection and the use of strong positioning sequences – their initial stability from favored 'phasing' may convert to high instability and disfavored 'phasing' after 5 bp of DNA translocation – which may underlie the progressive ejection observed with 601 nucleosomes.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative statement about the mechanism of nucleosome ejection, supported by a citation to prior work.

claims.claim: Robust remodeling of 601 H3 R40A nucleosomes by RSC2 was observed.
claims.source: Indeed, we found robust remodeling of 601 H3 R40A nucleosomes by RSC2 (Figure 4—figure supplement 5A and Figure 4—figure supplement 6 for quantification), and (by nuclease susceptibility) found that these nucleosomes remain largely wrapped (Figure 4—figure supplement 5B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from nucleosome sliding assays shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 5A.

claims.claim: 601 H3 R40A nucleosomes remain largely wrapped.
claims.source: Indeed, we found robust remodeling of 601 H3 R40A nucleosomes by RSC2 (Figure 4—figure supplement 5A and Figure 4—figure supplement 6 for quantification), and (by nuclease susceptibility) found that these nucleosomes remain largely wrapped (Figure 4—figure supplement 5B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from nuclease mapping shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 5B.

claims.claim: While the H3 R40A mutation can result in an open and more loosely wrapped nucleosome conformation, this can be overcome by a strong DNA positioning sequence.
claims.source: Our data support the model that while the H3 R40A mutation can result in an open and more loosely wrapped nucleosome conformation, this can be overcome by a strong DNA positioning sequence.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that 601 H3 R40A nucleosomes are remodeled efficiently by RSC2 and remain largely wrapped.

claims.claim: The αN helix H3 R40A mutation itself does not impair remodeling by RSC2 unless that mutation confers partial unwrapping due to the underlying DNA sequence.
claims.source: In addition, the data indicate that the αN helix H3 R40A mutation itself does not impair remodeling by RSC2 unless that mutation confers partial unwrapping due to the underlying DNA sequence.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the comparison of RSC2 remodeling of 5S H3 R40A nucleosomes (poor remodeling) versus 601 H3 R40A nucleosomes (robust remodeling).

claims.claim: The mapping data confirm that 5S nucleosomes produced with yeast octamers are less well-wrapped than 601 nucleosomes, and have DNA ends that are more susceptible to nuclease digestion.
claims.source: Lastly, our mapping data confirm that 5S nucleosomes produced with yeast octamers are less well-wrapped than 601 nucleosomes, and have DNA ends that are more susceptible to nuclease digestion.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from nuclease mapping shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 5 and Figure 4—figure supplement 5B.

claims.claim: RSC has been examined by chromatin co-immunoprecipitation (ChIP) in several formats.
claims.source: RSC has been examined by chromatin co-immunoprecipitation (ChIP) in several formats (Damelin et al., 2002; Yen et al., 2012; Vinayachandran et al., 2018; Brahma and Henikoff, 2019), though only one study has examined Rsc1/2 differences.
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claims.claim: An early ChIP approach with microarrays examined Rsc1 and Rsc2 differences, and revealed similar promoter targets for RSC1 and RSC2 complexes.
claims.source: This early ChIP approach with microarrays examined Rsc1 and Rsc2 differences, and revealed similar promoter targets for RSC1 and RSC2 complexes (Ng et al., 2002).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claims.claim: Recent examination of Sth1/RSC occupancy by the 'cut and run' MNase approach revealed general enrichment for RSC complexes at many +1 and −1 nucleosomes, as well as high enrichment of RSC within the NDR of genes with very wide NDRs (e.g., ribosomal protein genes).
claims.source: Recent examination of Sth1/RSC occupancy by the 'cut and run' MNase approach (which would have superimposed and not distinguished between Rsc1 and Rsc2 occupancy) revealed general enrichment for RSC complexes at many +1 and −1 nucleosomes, as well as high enrichment of RSC within the NDR of genes with very wide NDRs (e.g., ribosomal protein genes).
claims.evidence: This statement is based on prior work and is supported by the citation context.

claims.claim: Wide NDR regions/promoters have been shown to contain RSC bound to partially-unwrapped nucleosomes, rather than the complete lack of nucleosomes.
claims.source: Notably, these wide NDR regions/promoters have been shown to contain RSC bound to partially-unwrapped nucleosomes, rather than the complete lack of nucleosomes (Brahma and Henikoff, 2019).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claims.claim: RSC (Rsc1, Rsc2 and Rsc3) shows high occupancy at promoters with wide NDRs, with Rsc1 appearing more enriched than Rsc2.
claims.source: First, we observed high occupancy of RSC (Rsc1, Rsc2 and Rsc3; Figure 5A) at promoters with wide NDRs, with Rsc1 appearing more enriched than Rsc2.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from ChIP-seq shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: Hmo1 occupancy positively correlates with regions displaying the widest NDRs and bearing the highest Rsc1 and Rsc2 occupancy, with an apparent higher correlation with Rsc1.
claims.source: Notably, Hmo1 occupancy positively correlates with regions displaying the widest NDRs and bearing the highest Rsc1 and Rsc2 occupancy, with an apparent higher correlation with Rsc1 (Figure 5A–D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from ChIP-seq shown in Figure 5A-D.

claims.claim: The loci with the highest Hmo1 occupancy displayed a mean region size of 336 bp, and a remarkable two-thirds of those genes were ribosomal protein genes (RPGs).
claims.source: The loci with the highest Hmo1 occupancy displayed a mean region size of 336 bp, and a remarkable two-thirds of those genes were ribosomal protein genes (RPGs).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of ChIP-seq data.

claims.claim: Ribosomal protein gene promoters contain GC-rich sequences within their 'NDR' region, and Rsc3 enrichment is observed, consistent with Rsc3/30 involvement in targeting or retention.
claims.source: Ribosomal protein gene promoters contain GC-rich sequences within their 'NDR' region, and in keeping, we observe Rsc3 enrichment, consistent with Rsc3/30 involvement in targeting or retention.

claims.claim: Rsc1 complexes are markedly more enriched than Rsc2 complexes at tDNAs.

results.result: The Rsc3/30 heterodimer preferentially associates with the RSC1 complex via the CT2 domain (residues 617-777). This association is stoichiometric in RSC1 but substoichiometric in RSC2, and is maintained under high-salt stringency conditions for RSC1 but not RSC2.
results.evaluation: Claims C32-C40 are well-supported by multiple complementary experimental approaches including TAP purifications (Figure 1A-B), stringency testing (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), domain swap experiments (Figure 1C-E), and co-immunoprecipitation assays. The data consistently demonstrate preferential Rsc3/30 association with RSC1 and map this interaction to a specific region of the CT2 domain.

results.result: RSC1 and RSC2 complexes display similar DNA-dependent ATPase activities and nucleosome binding, but RSC1 shows markedly greater sliding activity than RSC2 on 5S nucleosomes. The Rsc3/30 module moderately inhibits remodeling activity of both complexes without affecting ATPase activity or nucleosome binding.
results.evaluation: Claims C44-C52 are supported by biochemical assays including ATPase measurements (Figure 2B), nucleosome sliding assays (Figure 2C), ATP-dependence controls (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A), and nucleosome binding assays (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B). The data demonstrate clear functional differences between RSC1 and RSC2 in remodeling partially-unwrapped nucleosomes while showing similar basic enzymatic activities.

results.result: The slower-migrating RSC remodeled product on native gels is an intact nucleosome containing H2A/H2B dimers, not a hexasome or tetrasome.
results.evaluation: Claim C53 is supported by experimental data using fluorescently labeled H2A (Oregon Green) showing that the H2A/H2B dimer to DNA ratio is maintained in the 'slid' band (Figure 2—figure supplement 3), ruling out hexasome or tetrasome formation.

results.result: Histone mutations that are lethal specifically with rsc1Δ map exclusively to the H3 αN helix region (DNA entry/exit site) and the H2A C-terminus. These mutations overlap strongly with those known to increase partial nucleosome unwrapping by FRET, suggesting RSC2 complexes have decreased ability to remodel partially-unwrapped nucleosomes.
results.evaluation: Claims C54-C58 are supported by comprehensive genetic screens (Table 1, Figure 3A-B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1) and correlation with published FRET data (Table 2). The genetic data provide strong evidence that rsc1Δ-specific synthetic lethality is associated with mutations that promote partial nucleosome unwrapping.

results.result: The CT2 domain of Rsc1 (specifically residues 617-777) can complement rsc1Δ αN helix histone synthetic lethality when placed in Rsc2. High-copy RSC3 or RSC30 suppresses the temperature-sensitive phenotype of rsc1Δ H3 V46A, linking Rsc3/30 association to management of partially-unwrapped nucleosomes.
results.evaluation: Claims C59-C62 are supported by domain swap complementation assays (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 2A) and high-copy suppression experiments (Figure 3D). These genetic approaches provide convergent evidence linking the Rsc1 CT2 domain and Rsc3/30 association to the ability to manage partially-unwrapped nucleosomes.

results.result: The H3 K56Q mutation (which promotes unwrapping) is lethal with rsc1Δ but not rsc2Δ, while K56A (which has little effect on unwrapping) shows no synthetic lethality. Domain swaps of bromodomains and BAH domains do not alter synthetic lethality patterns, indicating the phenotype is not linked to bromodomain-histone acetylation interactions.
results.evaluation: Claims C63-C67 are supported by genetic assays (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 2A-B) and correlation with published biochemical data on K56 mutations. The data effectively rule out bromodomain-acetylation interactions as the basis for the rsc1Δ-specific synthetic lethality and support an unwrapping-based mechanism.

results.result: RSC1 complexes are markedly more active than RSC2 complexes in sliding H3 R40A nucleosomes, despite both complexes binding these mutant nucleosomes similarly. This suggests the defect in RSC2 remodeling occurs after initial nucleosome engagement.
results.evaluation: Claims C68-C70 are supported by nucleosome sliding assays (Figure 3E) and binding assays (Figure 3—figure supplement 4). The data demonstrate that differential remodeling activity is not due to differences in nucleosome binding, supporting a post-binding mechanistic difference.

results.result: Wild-type 174 bp 5S yeast nucleosomes display asymmetric unwrapping with one fully-wrapped side and one partially-unwrapped side. H3 R40A nucleosomes show a much lower proportion of largely-wrapped species (≥135 bp) than wild-type, supporting that RSC1 manages partially-unwrapped nucleosomes better than RSC2.
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C75 are supported by ExoIII-S1 nuclease mapping with paired-end sequencing (Figure 3—figure supplement 5). The mapping data provide direct biochemical evidence for differential nucleosome wrapping and support the hypothesis that RSC1 is specialized for partially-unwrapped nucleosomes. However, C75 is speculative about the mechanism.

results.result: Synthetic phenotypes are observed in rsc1Δ hmo1Δ mutants but not rsc2Δ hmo1Δ mutants, suggesting greater reliance of Rsc2 on Hmo1 for functional cooperativity. This synthetic sickness is partially complemented by the Rsc1 CT2 domain and partially suppressed by high-copy RSC3 or RSC30.
results.evaluation: Claims C79-C81 are supported by genetic interaction assays (Figure 4A) and complementation/suppression experiments (Figure 4B). The data demonstrate functional interactions between Rsc1/2, Rsc3/30, and Hmo1 in managing partially-unwrapped nucleosomes.

results.result: Both Rsc1 and Rsc2 co-immunoprecipitate with Hmo1 on chromatin, but show differential functional/genetic interactions, with RSC2 complexes showing greater reliance on Hmo1.
results.evaluation: Claims C82-C83 are supported by co-immunoprecipitation experiments from crosslinked chromatin (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1) combined with the genetic interaction data. The data demonstrate both physical and functional interactions between RSC and Hmo1.

results.result: Hmo1 moderately stimulates RSC1 sliding activity but greatly stimulates RSC2 activity on 5S nucleosomes. Both RSC1 and RSC2 slide 5S nucleosomes at lower remodeler concentrations in the presence of Hmo1.
results.evaluation: Claims C85-C86 are supported by in vitro nucleosome sliding assays with purified Hmo1 (Figure 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement 2-3). The data demonstrate differential stimulation of RSC1 and RSC2 by Hmo1, consistent with the genetic interaction data.

results.result: RSC1 and RSC2 complexes both display robust sliding activity with 601 nucleosomes, with RSC1 activity slightly higher.
results.evaluation: Claim C87 is supported by nucleosome sliding assays with 601 nucleosomes (Figure 4E, Figure 4—figure supplement 4). The data show that both complexes remodel well-wrapped nucleosomes efficiently, in contrast to their differential activity on partially-unwrapped 5S nucleosomes.

results.result: RSC2 robustly remodels 601 H3 R40A nucleosomes, which remain largely wrapped despite the H3 R40A mutation. This indicates that strong DNA positioning sequences can overcome the unwrapping tendency of the H3 R40A mutation, and that the mutation itself does not impair RSC2 remodeling unless it confers partial unwrapping due to the underlying DNA sequence.
results.evaluation: Claims C89-C93 are supported by nucleosome sliding assays (Figure 4—figure supplement 5A) and nuclease mapping (Figure 4—figure supplement 5B). The data provide important mechanistic insight showing that DNA sequence context determines whether the H3 R40A mutation results in partial unwrapping and RSC2 remodeling defects.

results.result: RSC (Rsc1, Rsc2, and Rsc3) shows high occupancy at promoters with wide NDRs, with Rsc1 appearing more enriched than Rsc2. Hmo1 occupancy positively correlates with the widest NDRs and highest RSC occupancy, with apparent higher correlation with Rsc1. Two-thirds of genes with highest Hmo1 occupancy are ribosomal protein genes, which contain GC-rich sequences and show Rsc3 enrichment.
results.evaluation: Claims C98-C101 are supported by ChIP-seq data (Figure 5A-D). The genomic localization data are consistent with the biochemical and genetic findings, showing that RSC1, RSC2, Rsc3/30, and Hmo1 co-localize at promoters known to contain partially-unwrapped nucleosomes.

results.result: Rsc1 complexes are markedly more enriched than Rsc2 complexes at tDNAs, while Hmo1 is notably absent at these loci.
results.evaluation: Claims C102-C103 are supported by ChIP-seq data (Figure 5E-F). The data reveal a striking difference in Rsc1 versus Rsc2 occupancy at tDNAs, suggesting specialized functions for RSC1 at these loci.

results.result: Modest transcriptional differences are observed between WT, rsc1Δ, and rsc2Δ single mutants, but combining rsc1Δ or rsc2Δ with hmo1Δ results in strong transcriptional shifts affecting ~1000 genes. Ribosomal protein genes are among the most downregulated, and the transcriptional changes mirror environmental stress response patterns.
results.evaluation: Claims C106-C109 are supported by RNA-seq data (Figure 5G-H, Figure 5—figure supplement 1). The transcriptional data demonstrate functional redundancy between Rsc1 and Rsc2 in the presence of Hmo1, but reveal strong cooperative effects when both systems are impaired.

results.result: Rsc1 and Rsc2 both cooperate with Hmo1 to promote transcription of ribosomal protein genes, and chromatin remodeling at these growth-regulated loci requires the action of both Rsc1 and Rsc2 when Hmo1 is absent.
results.evaluation: Claims C110-C111 are inferences drawn from the RNA-seq data showing strong effects only in double mutants. The interpretation is well-supported by the data and consistent with the biochemical and genetic findings.

results.result: Only rsc2Δ rsc30Δ mutants strongly impact ribosomal protein gene expression, suggesting that the RSC1 complex is more reliant on Rsc3/30 than the RSC2 complex, and that in rsc2Δ rsc30Δ both complexes are impaired.
results.evaluation: Claims C112-C114 are supported by RNA-seq data (Figure 5—figure supplement 2). The genetic interaction pattern is consistent with the biochemical data showing preferential Rsc3/30 association with RSC1.

results.result: Phylogenetic analysis reveals that RSC2 is the more ancient ortholog, RSC3 appeared before the whole genome duplication (WGD), and the WGD created RSC1/2 and RSC3/30 paralogs along with ribosomal protein gene duplications. HMO1 predates RSC3 and the WGD. Specialization of Rsc1 to preferentially bind Rsc3/30 and regulate ribosomal protein genes was enabled by the WGD.
results.evaluation: Claims C115-C120 are supported by phylogenetic analysis (Figure 5—figure supplement 3) and established knowledge about yeast genome evolution. The evolutionary analysis provides context for understanding the functional specialization observed in the experimental data. However, C120 is somewhat speculative about the selective advantage.

results.result: RSC1 complexes have a higher intrinsic ability to mobilize partially-unwrapped nucleosomes compared to RSC2, augmented by partner proteins that preferentially assist either RSC1 (Rsc3/30) or RSC2 (Hmo1) complexes.
results.evaluation: Claims C121-C122 represent the main conclusions of the manuscript, integrating multiple lines of evidence from biochemical, genetic, and genomic experiments. The conclusions are well-supported by the comprehensive dataset presented.
